verdict.headline: This logistics contract has critical risks regarding exclusive foreign court jurisdiction and highly unbalanced commercial terms.
summary: The agreement is governed by Hong Kong law with exclusive jurisdiction in Hong Kong courts, meaning you must travel and pay high legal fees abroad to resolve any dispute.
The carrier's liability is capped at a tiny RM 50 per parcel and excludes perishable items like fresh flowers entirely, while they can unilaterally set fuel surcharges.
This contract is governed by the laws of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region; we check it against Malaysian law only as a fallback.

findings.title: Tiny fixed liability cap
findings.quote: The Carrier's liability for any loss of or damage to a Parcel, for delay, or for any other claim connected with that Parcel is limited to RM 50 per Parcel, regardless of the Declared Value of the Parcel and regardless of the cause of the loss.
findings.why_risky: The RM 50 limit is extremely low and does not reflect the actual value of your parcels. If a high-value parcel is lost, you will bear almost the entire loss.
findings.standard: A balanced liability cap should cover the actual declared value of the parcel up to a reasonable commercial limit, or be based on multiple months' fees.
findings.suggested_ask: Please increase the liability cap per parcel to match the Declared Value up to a limit of RM 500.

citations.title: Limitation of liability: the most either side can be made to pay (service agreement)
citations.excerpt: - **Mutual cap**: the same cap for both sides, usually **the fees paid or payable in the 12 months** before the claim. - **Mutual exclusion** of indirect losses (lost profits, lost business, loss of reputation) for both sides. - **Carve-outs from the cap** (amounts that stay uncapped or have a higher cap) apply to both sides equally: fraud, death or personal injury caused by negligence, breach...

findings.title: Discretionary fuel surcharge
findings.quote: fuel surcharge is set by the Carrier from time to time at its sole discretion and is notified on the Carrier's website. The Carrier is not required to link the fuel surcharge to any published fuel price.
findings.why_risky: The carrier can increase your shipping costs arbitrarily without any reference to actual fuel price movements. This creates absolute pricing uncertainty for your business.
findings.standard: Surcharges should be linked directly to a recognized public index, such as official retail fuel prices, using a transparent formula.
findings.suggested_ask: Please link the fuel surcharge to the Malaysian retail fuel price index using a transparent, published formula.

citations.title: Payment, late interest and price increases (service agreement)
citations.excerpt: - **Payment within 30 days** of a correct invoice (30-60 days is common in Malaysia and Singapore). - Prices stated **excluding tax**, with Malaysian service tax (SST) or Singapore GST added where it applies. - **Disputed invoices:** the customer may hold back the disputed part in good faith while paying the rest, and both sides try to resolve it quickly. - **Late interest** at a modest rate, r...

findings.title: Exclusive Hong Kong jurisdiction
findings.quote: Any dispute arising out of or in connection with this Agreement shall be submitted to the exclusive jurisdiction of the courts of Hong Kong. The Customer shall bear its own travel and legal costs.
findings.why_risky: You must travel and sue the carrier in Hong Kong for any local delivery dispute. This is highly impractical and cost-prohibitive for a Malaysian SME shipping local parcels.
findings.standard: The contract should be subject to the law and courts where the service is actually performed and where both parties operate.
findings.suggested_ask: Please make the agreement subject to Malaysian law and the courts of Kuala Lumpur, where both parties operate.

citations.title: Governing law: which country's law applies (service agreement)
citations.excerpt: - The law of the country where the **customer** receives the service, or where both sides are based. - Malaysian law with Kuala Lumpur courts, or Singapore law with Singapore courts, for a contract between companies in these two countries. - The courts named match the law chosen. - Non-exclusive jurisdiction, or arbitration in the region (see `dispute_resolution.md`).

missing_clauses.title: Service performance warranty
missing_clauses.why_it_matters: The contract does not promise any minimum standard of care or skill for delivery, leaving you with little recourse if delivery is repeatedly delayed or handled poorly.
missing_clauses.suggested_ask: Please add a warranty that the Services will be performed with reasonable care, skill, and diligence in accordance with industry standards.

verdict.headline: High-risk employment contract with excessive hours, unfair notice disparity, full training bond clawback, and void non-compete.
summary: The contract sets working hours above statutory limits without overtime pay, creates severe notice period imbalances, and imposes an un-prorated RM 15,000 training bond with broad wage deductions.
Clause 12.1 imposes a two-year post-employment non-compete across Southeast Asia, which under Malaysian law is generally void under section 28 of the Contracts Act 1950.
Several terms conflict with standard statutory protections under the Employment Act 1955, including notice equality and permitted wage deductions.

findings.title: Discretionary probation extension and notice disparity
findings.quote: The Company may extend the Probation Period at its sole discretion for such further period or periods as it thinks fit, by written notice to the Employee given at any time before the Probation Period (as extended) ends.
findings.why_risky: The company can prolong your probation indefinitely at its sole discretion without any fixed limit. Furthermore, clause 3.3 requires you to give 1 month's notice to resign during probation while the company can dismiss you on only 1 week's notice.
findings.standard: Probation should be for a fixed term (typically 3 to 6 months), extendable at most once for a defined duration with written reasons, with equal notice periods for both sides.
findings.suggested_ask: Please set probation at 3 months, allow one extension of up to 3 months only with written reasons and a fixed end date, and give both sides the same notice period during probation.

citations.title: Probation (employment)

verdict.headline: High-risk loan contract with daily compounding late fees, an illegal default interest hike, and unlimited guarantor liability.
summary: The contract imposes compounding late charges and raises interest to 24% on default, which conflicts with statutory limits under Malaysian moneylending rules.
The guarantee makes the guarantor liable for unlimited costs and future debts without notice or consent.
Upfront deduction of processing fees reduces proceeds while interest is charged on the gross principal.

findings.title: Daily compounding late fee
findings.quote: If an instalment is not paid when due, a late fee of 0.5% of the overdue amount is charged for each day it remains unpaid. The late fee for each day is added to the overdue amount at the end of that day, and the late fee for the following day is calculated on the new total, so that the late fee compounds daily until the overdue amount and all late fees are paid in full.
findings.why_risky: Compounding daily late charges can rapidly multiply the debt and conflict with statutory moneylending limits. Malaysian law generally prohibits compound interest on loans from licensed moneylenders.
findings.standard: Late fees should be modest, non-compounding simple charges on the overdue instalment only.
findings.suggested_ask: Please replace the daily compounding late fee in clause 4.1 with a simple, non-compounding late charge on the overdue instalment.
